section.title: The Proverbs of Solomon
section.sectionRationale: A new heading, 'The proverbs of Solomon,' marks the start of the book's first great collection of short, independent sayings, most of them built on antithetic parallelism, a righteous line set directly against a wicked one. Chapter 10 gathers thirty two such sayings around recurring themes, honest speech, diligent hands, and the LORD's blessing on the upright.
section.thesis: Where chapters 1 to 9 built sustained arguments, this new collection teaches wisdom proverb by proverb, contrasting the righteous and the wicked so sharply and repeatedly that the reader begins to see two whole ways of life, in work, speech, and destiny, standing behind every line.
section.frameNote: Four thematic clusters within the chapter's independent sayings: the wise and diligent household, verses 1 to 5; the righteous and wicked in speech, verses 6 to 14; wealth, work, and the tongue, verses 15 to 21; and the LORD's blessing and the destinies of the righteous and the wicked, verses 22 to 32.

verses.text: The proverbs of Solomon: A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son grief to his mother.
Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing, but righteousness brings deliverance from death.
The LORD does not let the {{tsaddiq|righteous}} go hungry, but He denies the craving of the {{rasha|wicked}}.
Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth.
He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son.
Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.
The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot.
A wise heart will receive commandments, but foolish lips will come to ruin.
He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.
He who winks the eye causes grief, and foolish lips will come to ruin.
The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked {{kesah|conceals}} violence.
Hatred stirs up dissension, but love {{kesah|covers}} all transgressions.
Wisdom is found on the lips of the discerning, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks judgment.
The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of the fool invites destruction.

units.label: Wealth, work, and the tongue
units.note: the ordinary economy of a life

verses.text: The wealth of the rich man is his fortified city, but poverty is the ruin of the poor.
The labor of the righteous leads to life, but the gain of the wicked brings punishment.
Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who ignores reproof goes astray.
The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever spreads slander is a fool.
When words are many, sin is unavoidable, but he who restrains his lips is wise.
The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, but the heart of the wicked has little worth.
The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of judgment.

units.label: The LORD's blessing and two destinies

verses.text: The blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it.
The fool delights in shameful conduct, but a man of understanding has wisdom.
What the wicked man dreads will overtake him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted.
When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the righteous are secure forever.
Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the slacker to those who send him.
The {{yirah|fear of the LORD}} prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be cut short.
The hope of the righteous is joy, but the expectations of the wicked will perish.
The way of the LORD is a refuge to the upright, but destruction awaits those who do evil.
The righteous will never be shaken, but the wicked will not inhabit the land.
The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but a perverse tongue will be cut out.
The lips of the righteous know what is fitting, but the mouth of the wicked is perverse.

tsaddiq.gloss: The righteous one, a person whose life is rightly ordered toward God and neighbor. Chapter 10 sets this figure against the wicked in almost every verse, showing righteousness less as flawless perfection and more as a settled, trustworthy direction of life.

rasha.gloss: The wicked one, whose life is bent against God's order, described here through hidden violence, hollow gain, and a name that will rot. The chapter's relentless contrast with the righteous is meant to make each reader ask which category truly describes them.

kesah.gloss: To cover or conceal, used twice in close proximity with opposite force, the wicked mouth conceals violence, verse 11, while love covers transgressions, verse 12. The same Hebrew root can hide evil or graciously overlook another's wrong, and the New Testament quotes verse 12 directly, 1 Peter 4:8.

yirah.gloss: The fear of the LORD, named in verse 27 as the very thing that prolongs life, tying this chapter's many contrasts of righteous and wicked back to the book's opening and recurring motto.

basic.context: With chapter 10, Proverbs shifts style entirely. Instead of long connected speeches, it now offers a rapid string of short, independent sayings, most built on a simple pattern, a line about the righteous set directly against a line about the wicked. Read together, these thirty two proverbs paint two whole trajectories of life, in family, work, speech, and ultimate destiny, and press the reader to notice which trajectory actually describes them.
basic.hermeneutics: Each verse here is a self contained proverb, not a paragraph in a developing argument, so the same theme, righteous versus wicked speech, work, or destiny, is revisited from many angles rather than argued once at length. These are general, typical observations about how life under God usually unfolds, not legal guarantees; the book itself, and Job and Ecclesiastes alongside it, shows that the righteous sometimes suffer and the wicked sometimes prosper for a season, without overturning the truth that God's moral order is real and ultimately vindicated.
basic.originalLanguages: Nearly every verse sets the tsaddiq, righteous, against the rasha, wicked, letting repetition do the teaching work a sustained argument would otherwise do. Verses 11 and 12 use the same root, kacah, to cover or conceal, for opposite ends, the wicked mouth conceals violence, while love covers transgressions, a wordplay the New Testament picks up directly, 1 Peter 4:8. And the chapter's closing section returns to yirah, the fear of the LORD, verse 27, tying its many contrasts back to the book's foundational motto.
basic.typology: Verse 12's picture of love covering all transgressions anticipates and is directly quoted in 1 Peter 4:8, and ultimately points to the greater covering of sin accomplished at the cross, where Christ's love did not merely overlook wrongdoing between neighbors but actually bore its penalty so it could be truly and finally covered.
basic.christ: The chapter's recurring picture of the righteous as secure, blessed, and a fountain of life, while the wicked face ruin, finds its deepest ground in Christ, the only truly righteous One, whose righteousness alone qualifies anyone to stand in the blessed category this chapter describes. And verse 12, love covers all transgressions, quoted directly in 1 Peter 4:8, points to a love that does not merely overlook sin between neighbors but, in Christ, actually bears its cost so that it can be truly covered forever.
basic.god: God is the source of every genuine blessing, verse 22, adding no sorrow to what He gives, and He is the moral foundation beneath this whole chapter's contrasts, the LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, verse 3, the way of the LORD is a refuge to the upright, verse 29. His fear, not mere cleverness, is what actually prolongs life, verse 27.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 4:8 quotes verse 12 nearly word for word, above all, love covers a multitude of sins. Matthew 12:34 to 37 teaches that words reveal the heart, echoing this chapter's many sayings on speech. Psalm 1 pictures the same two ways, righteous and wicked, that structure this whole chapter. Romans 5:19 grounds true righteousness in Christ's obedience, not human achievement.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's rapid fire contrasts between the righteous and the wicked summarize, in miniature, the whole Bible's story of two ways, one leading to life, one to ruin. That story finds its resolution in Christ, whose perfect righteousness alone qualifies sinners for the blessings this chapter describes, and whose covering love, quoted directly in the New Testament from verse 12, deals fully and finally with the sin no human effort can cover on its own.

context.literary:
The heading 'The proverbs of Solomon' in 10:1 marks a change of genre as sharp as any in the Bible. Chapters 1 to 9 were lectures: a father addressing 'my son' across many verses, building a case, telling a story. From here to 22:16 the book is a collection of individual sayings, each usually two lines long, each complete on its own. The effect is that of a gallery rather than a speech. The reader is expected to stop at each frame, turn it over and then move on.

The dominant device is the contrast. Most verses in this chapter set a line about the righteous against a line about the wicked, or the wise against the fool, joined by 'but.' A few break the pattern, such as verse 22, which continues with 'and,' and verse 26, which is a simile, 'Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes.' Because the pairs are short, the reader gets the sense of two roads without needing an argument for each, and the repetition across the chapter drives the point home.

The sayings are not randomly shuffled. The frame note groups them into clusters, and the clusters are linked by catchwords: 'conceals' in verses 6, 11 and 18, 'lips' in verses 8, 10, 13, 18, 19, 21 and 32, 'life' in verses 11, 16, 17 and 27, and 'mouth' through the middle of the chapter. A thread of speech runs from verse 6 to verse 21, and the last third gathers into themes of permanence and fear, with verse 27, 'The fear of the LORD prolongs life,' recalling the motto of 1:7 and 9:10.

Several lines are repeated in the chapter itself or elsewhere in the collection. The second half of verse 6 returns in verse 11, and the second half of verse 8 returns in verse 10. Verse 2 is echoed in 11:4, and verse 1 is almost repeated in 15:20. This reuse shows the editors working like curators who place familiar sayings in new neighbourhoods so that each shades the others.
context.historical:
The heading and the book's own notes give the setting. Proverbs 1:1 attributes the book to Solomon, and 1 Kings 4:32 says he composed three thousand proverbs. Proverbs 25:1 reports that 'the men of Hezekiah king of Judah' copied out further sayings of his, which shows that the collection was handed on and edited over centuries. The chapters in between include other voices, such as the 'sayings of the wise' in 24:23. The result is a book that bears Solomon's name as its head while it grew in the keeping of the royal court and its scribes.

The world these sayings assume is mostly the world of the household. A father's joy and a mother's grief over a son, verse 1, are about the standing of a family in a village. Food depends on a harvest that must be gathered in its season, verse 5. A man who 'sleeps during harvest' is not just lazy but a danger to his family, since the grain would not wait. Idle hands lead to poverty, verse 4, in an economy with little safety net. The 'fortified city' of verse 15 describes a rich man's wealth as a refuge, and the ruin of the poor is the plain fact of having nothing to fall back on.

Speech mattered in a society where reputation and trust were the currency. A winking eye, verse 10, a concealed hatred, verse 18, and slander could undo a family's name in a small community. The 'name of the wicked will rot,' verse 7, speaks to a culture in which a name was kept alive through descendants and memory. The messenger of verse 26 recalls the age before post and telephones: an unreliable errand boy was as irritating as vinegar or smoke, because there was no other way to send word.

Land lay at the heart of Israel's hope. The promise that 'the wicked will not inhabit the land,' verse 30, would be heard against the covenant gift of Canaan and the warning of exile. A first hearer would feel in these words the weight of Deuteronomy's blessings and curses.
context.canonical:
Chapter 10 belongs to the two-ways teaching that runs from Psalm 1 to the Sermon on the Mount. Psalm 1 sets the blessed man beside the wicked who are like chaff, Psalm 1:4 to 6, and Proverbs 10 spells the same contrast out in dozens of settings. Psalm 37:9 to 11 promises that the meek will inherit the land, and Proverbs 10:30 states the other side, that the wicked will not dwell in it. Jeremiah 17:7 and 8 compares the one who trusts in the LORD to a tree by water, and Proverbs 10:11 calls the mouth of the righteous a fountain of life, an image repeated in 13:14 and 14:27.

The book that contains this chapter also contains its own corrective. Proverbs 16:1 and 2 reminds the reader that the heart's plans and verdicts belong to the LORD, and Job and Ecclesiastes press on the exceptions, Job 21:7 to 13 and Ecclesiastes 8:14. A good reading of chapter 10 keeps all of them in view, reading the sayings as the truth about how God's world tends to run and the rest of Scripture as a check against a mechanical use of them.

The New Testament draws on many of the verses. Peter quotes 10:12 when he says that love covers a multitude of sins, 1 Peter 4:8, and James uses it near the end of his letter, James 5:20. Jesus' warning about the careless word and the overflow of the heart, Matthew 12:34 to 37 and Luke 6:45, repeats the teaching on the mouth in 10:11 and 10:20. The wise builder whose house stands in the storm, Matthew 7:24 to 27, is a picture of verse 25, 'When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the righteous are secure forever.' Paul's call to speak what is helpful, Ephesians 4:29, and to let speech be gracious, Colossians 4:6, applies the chapter's counsel to the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The collectors of these sayings wanted a young Israelite to take in a whole way of seeing, one proverb at a time. The earlier chapters had told him that wisdom matters. This chapter shows him what it looks like at the breakfast table, in the field, on the market street and in the talk of a town. The aim is to form a character who instinctively recognises the wise path in the thousand small decisions no lecture could name in advance.

The sages also meant the contrast to be sharp. The righteous and the wicked are drawn in clean lines because the sayings are meant to be remembered and applied, not to supply a clinical analysis of every real life. The sharpness is a teaching tool. It tells the learner that his choices lead somewhere, that talk, work and trust are not neutral, and that over a lifetime they sort a person into one of two kinds.

At bottom they wanted him to see that the moral order is God's order. The sayings are full of what the LORD does, verse 3, verse 22, verse 27, verse 29, and they keep returning to the fear of the LORD. A reader who took the chapter as a manual for success without God would have missed what the collectors put at its foundation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of these sayings are descriptions. 'The wealth of the rich man is his fortified city, but poverty is the ruin of the poor,' verse 15, reports what wealth does in a world that offers the poor no cushion. It does not say that wealth is the best refuge, and the book soon says otherwise, Proverbs 18:10 and 11. 'The fool delights in shameful conduct,' verse 23, is a portrait, not a command to be unamused.

Others are prescriptions in disguise. A proverb that praises the wise son who gathers in summer, verse 5, is a call to be that son. A saying that sets the restraint of the lips against the multiplication of words, verse 19, invites the listener to learn restraint. The reader's task is to hear the invitation inside the observation and to see which sayings tell us how things are and which tell us how to live.

Applying the chapter calls for care about its promises. 'The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry,' verse 3, is a statement of the way God's world generally runs, and the same book and Job both show righteous people who suffer lack. The sayings state the typical case and trust the whole of Scripture to supply the exceptions. They should neither be read as guarantees for each person nor dismissed as naive. They are true in the way a map is true: reliable on the whole, and meant for a traveller who keeps watching the road.

debates.question: Are the sayings promises, rules of thumb, or reports of a moral order?

views.label: Promises
views.case: Some read statements like verse 3, 24 or 27 as guarantees from God that obedience brings prosperity and long life. The text seems to support them with its confident language, for example 'the desire of the righteous will be granted,' verse 24.

views.label: General rules of thumb
views.case: Others point out that Proverbs 10 itself contains the clues that these are generalisations. Job 21:7 to 13 and Ecclesiastes 8:14 describe the wicked prospering and the righteous suffering, and the Psalms regularly cry out over the same problem, Psalm 73:3 to 5. Proverbs is a book about patterns, not contracts.

views.label: Reports of a moral order that God upholds
views.case: A third reading sees in the sayings a built-in tendency of actions to bring their consequences, with God overseeing the result. Verses 3, 22 and 29 name the LORD as the one who acts. On this view the sayings describe a world with a grain to it, and God keeps it running in that direction.

debates.bearing: The second and third views fit together. The sayings describe real tendencies that God upholds, and the rest of the Bible keeps the reader from turning those tendencies into a machine. The ultimate vindication of the righteous, which the chapter hints at in verses 25 and 30, awaits the day God sets everything right.

debates.question: Does verse 22 mean no sorrow comes with the LORD's blessing, or that toil adds nothing to it?

views.label: No sorrow attends the blessing
views.case: The Hebrew word etsev can mean sorrow or pain, and the BSB reads 'He adds no sorrow to it.' On this view wealth that God gives does not bring the anguish that wealth gained by fraud or greed brings, a theme of Proverbs 10:2 and 15:16.

views.label: Toil adds nothing to it
views.case: The same noun can mean painful labour, and some translations read the line as 'and toil adds nothing to it.' The point then is that the blessing does not depend on anxious striving. The word is related to the 'toil' of Genesis 3:17, so the verse may signal a relief from the curse of Eden.

debates.bearing: Either way the verse gives God the credit and takes away the anxiety. It does not excuse laziness, because verses 4 and 5 stand close by, but it teaches that enrichment comes from the LORD's hand and that He gives it without the bitterness that goes with grasping.

debates.question: What does 'the mouth of the wicked conceals violence' mean in verses 6 and 11?

views.label: Their speech hides violent intent
views.case: On the BSB reading, the wicked say pleasant things while planning harm. The line is then a warning that smooth words may cover a hostile heart, as in the 'lying lips' of verse 18.

views.label: Violence covers their mouth
views.case: The BSB footnote offers 'violence covers the mouth of the wicked.' The grammar allows the violence to be the subject, so that the sentence says that the harm they do closes their mouths or overwhelms what they say. The contrast is then with the blessings on the head of the righteous in the first line.

debates.bearing: The line is intentionally compact. Both readings are true of the wicked: they conceal, and violence consumes them. The repetition of the line in verse 11 suggests that the sages enjoyed the double edge.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter uses more than one word for the fool, and the difference helps. In verse 1 the 'foolish son' is a kesil, the dull, thick-headed type who will not learn. The 'foolish lips' of verses 8, 10 and 14 and the 'fools' of verse 21 come from evil, a related but different word used in 1:7, 'fools despise wisdom and discipline.' The kesil is usually drawn as dull and stubborn, the evil as headstrong and quarrelsome, and the person who 'lacks judgment' in verses 13 and 21 is chasar lev, 'lacking heart,' the same phrase that described the young man of Proverbs 7:7 and the guests of 9:4 and 9:16. The last occurrence in 10:21 gives the end of that road: such people 'die for lack of judgment.'

The word 'integrity' in verse 9 is tom, wholeness, and the one who walks in it 'walks securely,' betach, a word from the root that gives 'trust' in Proverbs 3:5. Security and trust are the same family. The man who is whole before God has no need to look behind him. The opposite is the one who 'perverts his ways,' a verb that means to twist, and he 'will be found out,' literally 'be known.' What was hidden becomes known.

Verse 12 sets two verbs against each other. Hatred 'stirs up' dissension, and love 'covers all transgressions.' The noun is pesha, the word for rebellious wrongs and not just slips, so the verse makes a strong claim. Proverbs 17:9 states it again, 'Whoever conceals an offense promotes love.' Peter, 1 Peter 4:8, and James, James 5:20, both draw on this verse. It is worth noticing that 'covers' is the same verb that appears in verses 6 and 11 for the wicked's mouth covering violence. The verb is the same, and the aims opposite: one covers in order to harm, the other to heal.

Verse 7 says the name of the wicked 'will rot.' The verb is raqav, which is used of wood decaying, and the noun is used of 'rot in the bones' in Proverbs 12:4 and 14:30. A name that decays is a vivid contrast to the memory of the righteous, which is 'a blessing.' Psalm 112:6 shares the thought, 'the righteous man will be remembered forever.'

In verse 25 the BSB's 'secure forever' translates a Hebrew phrase that reads, more literally, 'the righteous is an everlasting foundation.' It is the image behind Jesus' house on the rock, Matthew 7:24 and 25. Two other words in the chapter belong together. In verses 15 and 29 the rich man's 'fortified city' and the LORD's 'refuge' both come from the root for strength, oz. The sage sets two strongholds side by side, the one a man builds from his wealth and the one God provides in His way.

Finally, 'brings forth' in verse 31 is a verb that means to bear fruit, as in Psalm 92:14, where the righteous 'still bear fruit' in old age, and the 'perverse tongue' will be 'cut out,' the verb for cutting down a tree. The mouth is pictured as an orchard that bears fruit for the righteous and is felled for the perverse.

typology.type: The righteous one who is a foundation, 10:25
typology.fulfillment: The Hebrew of verse 25 can be read 'the righteous is an everlasting foundation,' and when the storm passes, only the righteous remain. Jesus uses the same image of a house on the rock that stands against rain, torrents and wind, Matthew 7:24 to 27, and Paul says 'no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 3:11. The escalation is from a righteous person who endures to the righteous One on whom all others stand. The type falls short because no ordinary righteous person is a foundation for anyone else, while Christ is.

Love covers the offences that hatred would stir up, and the New Testament applies this to the community, 1 Peter 4:8. At its deepest level, the covering of sin is God's work. 'Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered,' Psalm 32:1, and Christ 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. The escalation is that the covering is atonement and not just forbearance: the sin is not ignored but borne. The type falls short because human love can cover a neighbour's slight but cannot pay for rebellion.

typology.type: The mouth of the righteous as a fountain of life, 10:11
typology.fulfillment: Proverbs says the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, and elsewhere that the teaching of the wise and the fear of the LORD are the same, Proverbs 13:14 and 14:27. The psalmist says that with God 'is the fountain of life,' Psalm 36:9. Jesus promises that the water He gives 'will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14, and calls on the thirsty to come to Him, John 7:37 and 38. The escalation is from a wise person whose words refresh to the One in whom the spring is found. The type falls short because the words of wise people can only direct to life, and Christ gives it.

typology.type: The one whose righteousness is secure, 10:2 and 10:16
typology.fulfillment: The proverbs promise that righteousness delivers from death and that the labour of the righteous leads to life. No sinner has a righteousness of this kind, which is why Paul says righteousness 'from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ,' Romans 3:22, and that 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. Christ 'has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness,' 1 Corinthians 1:30. The pattern holds, the escalation is that the righteousness is received, and the type falls short as a model of human achievement.

study.christ:
This chapter does not mention a coming king or a suffering servant, and it would be a mistake to look for one. What it does is describe the kind of person God's world was made to bless, the righteous, the wise, the one who walks in integrity, and in doing so it opens a question that the New Testament answers. Who is that person?

The first answer is that Jesus is. Of all the people who ever lived, He alone is the righteous man of these sayings. His mouth was a fountain of life, John 4:14 and 7:38, in a way that no other mouth has been. Peter says that no deceit was found in His mouth, 1 Peter 2:22, and the verse sets the sinless speech of Jesus beside the foolish lips of 10:8 and 10:14. He walked in integrity, and so walked securely, even to the cross, where He trusted Himself to the Father. His memory is a blessing in a sense that Proverbs can hardly have foreseen, because it is the memory of the One in whom the nations are blessed.

The second answer is that Jesus makes others righteous. The blessings of the chapter are for the righteous, and the Bible tells us frankly that none is righteous in himself, Romans 3:10 to 12 and 23. Paul's answer is that God gives a righteousness apart from the law, through faith in Christ, Romans 3:21 and 22. 'Through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. Isaiah looked ahead to the Servant who 'will justify many,' Isaiah 53:11. So the promises of Proverbs 10 become the portion of the believer, not by achievement but by being united to the righteous One. Paul can say He has become 'our righteousness,' 1 Corinthians 1:30.

The third answer concerns verse 12, 'love covers all transgressions.' Human love can overlook a neighbour's fault, but there is a covering that human love cannot make, the covering of rebellion before a holy God. The gospel is that the covering was made by the One who bore the sins in His own body, 1 Peter 2:24. When Peter quotes this proverb, he calls believers to imitate on a small scale what Christ did on the largest.

The fourth answer concerns the foundation. Verse 25 holds that when the storm passes only the righteous stand, and Jesus calls that stability a house built on His words, Matthew 7:24 to 27. Paul adds that He is Himself the foundation, 1 Corinthians 3:11. The chapter's picture of an unshakeable life finds its source in a Person.

A caution is in order. The chapter's thirty-two sayings are not thirty-two prophecies. They do not gain their meaning by being allegorised, and the lazy son of verse 5 is not a code for anything. They point to Christ by the shape of the righteous life they praise, and by the New Testament's own use of verses 12 and 25.
study.god:
The God of Proverbs 10 is the one who stands behind the order of ordinary life. He is named less often than the human actors in the chapter, but when He is named it is at the hinges. The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, verse 3. His blessing enriches, verse 22. The fear of Him prolongs life, verse 27. His way is a refuge to the upright, verse 29. The rest of the sayings, about the hand and the tongue and the harvest, are set within this framework, so that no ordinary event is outside His care.

He is the giver of every real blessing, and He gives without a hidden price. Verse 22 insists that the LORD's blessing comes with no sorrow added, whether that means no anguish or no desperate toil. The Bible's God is not a stingy bargainer who hands out gifts with a catch. He is the one who 'enriches,' and the wealth He gives is of a kind that does not rot the person who holds it.

He is the guardian of moral order. The chapter says that ill-gotten treasures profit nothing, verse 2, that what the wicked dread overtakes them, verse 24, and that the years of the wicked are cut short, verse 27. This is not the language of a world on its own. It is the language of a God who sees. Yet it is held beside the knowledge, expressed by the rest of Scripture, that He is patient and that His final verdict often awaits the end of the story.

He is the strength of His people. The 'refuge' of verse 29 is a stronghold, and in the same chapter the rich man's wealth is a fortified city. The writer sets human security beside divine security so that the reader can weigh them. The comparison is developed in Proverbs 18:10 and 11, where the name of the LORD is a strong tower and the rich man's wall is imagined.

He is the one who values truthful speech. Verse 18 condemns the one who conceals hatred with lying lips, and verse 31 promises that a perverse tongue will be cut out. It is hard to hear this and not think of the God of truth who cannot lie, and who wants His people to be known by what they say.

For worship, the chapter calls for two things. Thanksgiving: every good harvest, every wise child and every bit of peace in a life is a gift from the LORD's hand, verse 22. And trust: the God who is a refuge to the upright is the one to whom the righteous run, and the way they run to Him, as verse 27 says, is in the fear of the LORD.

crossReferences.note: The psalm contrasts the blessed man, who delights in the law and is like a tree by streams, with the wicked who are like chaff driven by the wind. Proverbs 10 fills in the same two ways with daily detail. Verse 25's whirlwind and the 'chaff' of Psalm 1:4 describe the same end for the wicked.

Evildoers will be cut off, and the meek will inherit the land. Proverbs 10:30 says it in a line: the righteous will never be shaken, but the wicked will not inhabit the land. The psalm explains how the righteous can wait, and the proverb gives the summary.

'Riches are worthless in the day of wrath, but righteousness brings deliverance from death' repeats the second half of 10:2 almost word for word. The editors of the collection set these two sayings in neighbouring chapters, and the effect is to underline that wealth cannot buy what only righteousness can supply.

The name of the LORD is a strong tower and the rich man's wealth is his fortified city, but only in his imagination a high wall. This pairs with 10:15 and 10:29 to show the two strongholds. Chapter 10 states the facts of money, and chapter 18 says which refuge actually holds.

Job describes the wicked living on, growing old and prosperous, and going down to Sheol in peace. It is the honest counterexample to sayings like 10:27 and 10:30, and it shows that Scripture does not expect the proverbs to cover every case. Reading them together keeps the proverbs from being used as a formula.

Peter quotes the heart of Proverbs 10:12 when he tells believers to love one another deeply because love covers a multitude of sins. The apostle applies the proverb to church life. The BSB footnote at 10:12 itself points here, which marks this as one of the clearest uses of a proverb in the New Testament.

Jesus says the mouth speaks from the overflow of the heart and that people will answer for every careless word. This takes the chapter's many sayings about lips and tongues, such as 10:11, 10:19 and 10:31, and states the principle behind them: speech is the surface of the heart.

James warns that the tongue, though small, steers the whole life and can set a forest ablaze. This echoes 10:19, 'When words are many, sin is unavoidable.' James adds what the proverb implies, that the tongue is hard to tame, and the answer to that comes from beyond ourselves.

The wise man builds on the rock, and when rain, torrents and winds come, his house stands, while the house on sand collapses. This is the parable form of 10:25, where the whirlwind passes and the wicked are no more. Jesus makes the foundation His own words.

The curse speaks of pain in childbirth and of toil in the ground. The noun for toil is related to the word in Proverbs 10:22, 'He adds no sorrow to it.' The proverb suggests that the LORD's blessing reaches into the world of the curse and lightens it.

'A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish man despises his mother' is nearly a copy of 10:1. The repetition shows how the collection places familiar proverbs in new settings, and the small differences, 'despises' for 'grief,' show that the sages shaped even their repetitions.

Paul tells believers to let no unwholesome talk come out of their mouths, only what builds up. He applies the wisdom of 10:11 and 10:21, where the mouth of the righteous is a fountain and its lips feed many, to the life of the church, and gives it its purpose: grace to those who listen.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world in which the words of God made everything and the first humans were given a good place to work and a clear word to keep. Genesis 3 shows the breaking of that word, and with it the first experience of toil, thorns and death. Proverbs 10 is written for people who live on the far side of that story. It teaches them how to live in a world that still carries God's design but is marked by the curse, where work is hard, words wound and wealth can fail. The sayings about diligent hands, honest speech and the fear of the LORD are an attempt to walk wisely in Eden's ruins.

Within the story of Israel, the chapter belongs to the covenant life. The land is the setting, verse 30, the blessing is conditioned on faithfulness, verse 22, and the fate of the wicked is the fate of the people who forget God. Deuteronomy had set before Israel blessing and curse, and the proverbs bring that choice down to the level of the workshop and the table. The wisdom writers stand with the prophets in saying that how a person speaks, works and trusts is part of how they stand with God.

But the Bible does not stop with the proverbs. Job and Ecclesiastes show that the sayings, though true, cannot explain every life. The exile showed that a nation could fail to be the righteous people the chapter pictures. These pressures raise the question the New Testament answers: where is the truly righteous person? In Jesus, whose mouth was a fountain of life, who walked in integrity, who bore the transgressions that love covers, and who is the foundation that survives the storm. By faith His people share His righteousness, Romans 5:19.

The new creation is the world in which Proverbs 10 comes fully true. The righteous will 'inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, in the meaning that verse 30 held out. The meek will 'delight in abundant prosperity,' Psalm 37:11, and nothing will be added to the blessing but joy, verse 22. The tongue will be healed, for the redeemed speak only truth. There will be no more curse, Revelation 22:3, and the fear of the LORD, which prolonged life in a fallen world, will be the gladness of those who see His face and live.

quiz.q: What literary form dominates chapter 10, and how does it differ from chapters 1 to 9?

options.text: Short, independent proverbs, mostly contrasting the righteous and the wicked, replacing the sustained discourses of chapters 1 to 9.
options.note: This marks the clear stylistic shift the heading in verse 1 signals.

options.text: Long narrative stories, just like chapters 1 to 9.
options.note: Chapter 10 moves away from narrative and sustained argument into short independent sayings.

options.text: Legal case rulings similar to the Law of Moses.
options.note: These are wisdom proverbs, not legal rulings or case law.

options.text: Personal letters addressed to named individuals.
options.note: The sayings are general proverbs, not personal correspondence, though many are addressed generally as if to a son elsewhere in the book.

quiz.q: How does verse 12 use the same Hebrew root, kacah, with opposite force compared to verse 11?

options.text: Verse 11 says the wicked mouth conceals violence, while verse 12 says love covers transgressions, the same word used to hide evil or graciously overlook wrong.
options.note: This wordplay is exact, and 1 Peter 4:8 quotes verse 12 directly.

options.text: The two verses use entirely unrelated words with no connection.
options.note: They share the same root, kacah, deliberately used with contrasting force.

options.text: Both verses describe the wicked exclusively.
options.note: Verse 12 specifically contrasts hatred with love, not two wicked descriptions.

options.text: Verse 12 is quoted in the Gospels, not in 1 Peter.
options.note: The direct New Testament quotation of this verse is in 1 Peter 4:8, not the Gospels.

quiz.q: How should proverbs like verse 3, 'the LORD does not let the righteous go hungry,' be understood?

options.text: As a general, typical description of God's moral order, not an unconditional promise against every exception.
options.note: Job and Ecclesiastes show real exceptions, so proverbs describe the normal pattern, not an ironclad guarantee for every case.

options.text: As an absolute guarantee with no exceptions anywhere in Scripture.
options.note: Job explicitly shows a righteous man suffering great want, contradicting a reading of total exception free guarantee.

options.text: As a statement with no real truth or usefulness at all.
options.note: The proverb reflects a real and trustworthy pattern of God's care, even though it is general rather than absolute.

options.text: As applicable only to New Testament believers, not Old Testament Israel.
options.note: The proverb's original audience was Israel, and its general principle of God's provision runs through both testaments, not one alone.

quiz.q: What does verse 27 identify as the key to a prolonged life?

options.text: The fear of the LORD.
options.note: This is stated directly and ties the chapter back to the book's opening motto in 1:7.

options.text: Financial wealth alone.
options.note: The verse specifically names the fear of the LORD, not wealth, as the key.

options.text: Physical strength and youth.
options.note: The verse's concern is moral and spiritual, not physical vigor.

options.text: Political power and influence.
options.note: The verse names fearing the LORD, not political standing, as decisive.

quiz.q: How does verse 12's teaching on love ultimately point to Christ?

options.text: Christ's atoning love does not merely overlook sin between people but bears its full penalty so it can be truly covered.
options.note: This connects the proverb, quoted in 1 Peter 4:8, to the deeper covering accomplished at the cross.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ or the New Testament.
options.note: 1 Peter 4:8 quotes this verse directly, showing a clear New Testament connection.

options.text: It teaches that love excuses sin without any real cost.
options.note: The gospel's covering of sin comes at real cost, the cross, not a mere excusing without payment.

options.text: It applies only to romantic relationships.
options.note: The proverb's scope is broader, covering wrongs between any people, and 1 Peter applies it to the whole Christian community.

questions: This chapter contrasts the righteous and the wicked in speech, work, and destiny. Which specific contrast in this chapter, honest versus deceptive speech, diligence versus laziness, hit closest to home for you today?

Verse 12 says love covers a multitude of sins, later quoted by Peter. Is there a wrong done against you that you are holding onto rather than covering with love, and what would it look like to release it?
Verse 19 warns that when words are many, sin is unavoidable. Where in your life could restraining your speech prevent unnecessary harm or conflict this week?
Verse 27 says the fear of the LORD prolongs life. How does reverence for God actually shape your daily choices, versus being just a phrase you agree with in theory?
This chapter's confidence in the righteous only holds fully true in Christ's righteousness credited to us. Where do you need to rest in His righteousness today rather than your own performance?

translationNotes.note: The second half of this verse can also be rendered 'but violence covers the mouth of the wicked,' a variation that reverses subject and verb but preserves the same basic contrast; the same variant reading applies to verse 11.
This verse can also be rendered 'but babbling fools will fall,' an alternate reading of the second half.
This verse is quoted nearly word for word in 1 Peter 4:8, 'above all, love covers a multitude of sins,' one of the clearest direct New Testament citations of Proverbs.
